reason: The water and phospholipids suggest forming the cell's outer boundary.
expectation: The phospholipids will arrange into a membrane in water.

effect: The phospholipids formed a lipid bilayer, which looks ready to surround the cell contents.
reaction: The picture makes the boundary's arrangement clear.
reason: The bilayer and cell contents appear to be the parts needed to make a cell boundary.
expectation: The bilayer will surround the cell contents to form a cell.

effect: The bilayer now surrounds the cell contents, and the boundary has slots for a channel and a pump.
reaction: The labeled slots make the next fittings clear.
reason: The channel protein matches the boundary's Channel slot.
expectation: The channel protein will fit into the cell boundary.

effect: The channel protein is installed, leaving the pump fitting to complete.
reason: The ion pump matches the remaining Pump slot.
expectation: The ion pump will fit into the cell boundary.

effect: The channel and pump are installed, completing the exchange-route goal; the next goal is to make a fuel-admitting protein.
reaction: The new goal gives the remaining gene a clear purpose.
reason: RNA polymerase reads DNA to make RNA, so the highlighted transporter gene looks like the starting point.
expectation: RNA polymerase will use the transporter gene to produce messenger RNA, with RNA building blocks if needed.

effect: The transporter gene has been copied into messenger RNA, which can carry its instructions to the ribosome.
reaction: The picture clearly explains why the DNA stays in the nucleus.
reason: The messenger RNA carries the protein instructions to the ribosome, and amino acids are available for building the chain.
expectation: The ribosome will use the messenger RNA and amino acids to make a protein chain.

effect: The ribosome used the messenger RNA and amino acids to make a glucose transporter chain. The chain appears to need folding and targeting before it can work.
reaction: The result makes the link between the RNA instructions and the protein chain clear.
reason: The folding and targeting machinery is the remaining piece that appears suited to preparing the transporter chain.
expectation: The chain will fold into a glucose transporter and be directed toward the cell membrane.

effect: The chain is now a folded glucose transporter in a membrane vesicle, ready to be fitted into the cell boundary.
reaction: The vesicle makes the targeting step visible, although its destination is implied.
reason: The transporter needs to reach the cell boundary to admit glucose.
expectation: The transporter will join the cell boundary and provide a route for glucose.

effect: The transporter joined the membrane and completed the fuel-admission goal. The result connects protein production to a change in what can cross the cell boundary.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the transporter reach the membrane, with the earlier channel and pump still visible.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making messenger RNA from the gene was the most worthwhile action: the result explained how instructions reach a ribosome while DNA stays in the nucleus.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the channel and pump was predictable because the slots named them. The picture compared their movement of ions, but the fitting results themselves added little explanation.

surprise.text: The folded transporter first appeared in a vesicle, then that vesicle joined the membrane. This made its route to the boundary more concrete.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary. The folding and targeting machinery had a clear role, though its destination was implied until the final result.

continue.text: I would continue into another chapter to see how this working cell connects to tissues and body systems. The sequence was clear, though several fittings were predictable.
